blocks.text: Benchmark evaluation runs a fine-tuned model against a fixed, standardized set of questions with known correct answers, producing a score that can be compared directly against other models, an approach distinct from the per-example metrics like BLEU, ROUGE, and exact match covered in earlier topics of this module.
This topic covers what a benchmark actually is, several widely used examples, and the practical pitfalls, particularly data contamination, that come with relying on standardized benchmark scores.
1. What a Benchmark Actually Is

blocks.alt: A standardized test set is a fixed set of questions with gold answers

blocks.text: A benchmark is a fixed, publicly defined set of questions or tasks paired with known correct answers, designed so that any model can be evaluated on exactly the same test and the resulting scores can be meaningfully compared across different models and research groups.
2. A Few Widely Used Benchmarks

blocks.alt: MMLU covers broad knowledge, HellaSwag covers commonsense, HumanEval covers code, GSM8K covers math

blocks.text: Different benchmarks target different capabilities, MMLU tests broad academic and professional knowledge across many subjects, HellaSwag tests commonsense reasoning about everyday situations, HumanEval tests code generation correctness, and GSM8K tests grade school level math word problem solving, each giving a narrow but standardized window into a specific capability.

blocks.text: 3. Running a Model Through a Benchmark

blocks.alt: A model under test runs on the fixed question set and gets scored against gold answers

blocks.text: Running a benchmark evaluation means feeding a model the exact same fixed set of questions the benchmark defines, collecting its answers, and scoring them against the known gold answers, typically using exact match, covered in the previous topic, or a task specific scoring function for something like code correctness.
4. Zero-Shot vs Few-Shot Evaluation

blocks.alt: Zero shot evaluation with no examples is compared against few shot evaluation with examples

blocks.text: Benchmarks can be run zero-shot, giving the model only the question with no example demonstrations, or few-shot, including a handful of example question and answer pairs in the prompt first, results can differ significantly between the two settings, so it matters which one a reported score actually used.

code.content:
# Zero-shot: just the question
prompt_zero_shot = "Question: What is the capital of France?\nAnswer:"

# Few-shot: a couple of examples first, then the real question
prompt_few_shot = (
    "Question: What is the capital of Japan?\nAnswer: Tokyo\n\n"
    "Question: What is the capital of Germany?\nAnswer: Berlin\n\n"
    "Question: What is the capital of France?\nAnswer:"
)

blocks.text: 5. Leaderboards and Model Comparison

blocks.alt: Model A scores 78 percent and Model B scores 82 percent on a leaderboard

blocks.text: Benchmark scores from many different models are commonly aggregated into public leaderboards, letting teams compare a newly fine-tuned model against known baselines and competing models on the exact same standardized test, a useful sanity check beyond internal evaluation alone.
6. The Data Contamination Problem

blocks.alt: Benchmark questions posted online can leak into training data, producing an inflated score

blocks.text: Because benchmark questions and answers are often published openly online, they can accidentally end up inside a model pretraining or fine-tuning data, a model that has effectively memorized benchmark answers scores artificially high without genuinely having the underlying capability the benchmark was meant to measure.

blocks.title: Contamination is a known, serious issue across the field
blocks.content: Several published analyses have found measurable overlap between popular benchmark questions and common pretraining datasets, a reason to treat unusually high benchmark scores with some skepticism, especially without knowing exactly what data a model was trained on.

blocks.text: 7. Why a Single Benchmark Score Is Not Enough

blocks.alt: A single benchmark score is compared against a full suite of benchmarks

blocks.text: Any individual benchmark measures a fairly narrow slice of capability, a model can score well on one benchmark while performing poorly on tasks that benchmark simply does not cover, using a broad suite spanning knowledge, reasoning, code, and math gives a much more complete picture than relying on any single number.
8. Benchmarks vs Task-Specific Evaluation

Standardized benchmarks are useful for comparing general capability across models, but they rarely reflect the exact distribution of a specific production use case, task-specific evaluation using metrics like BLEU, ROUGE, or human evaluation, all covered elsewhere in this module, on data that actually resembles production usage often matters more for a real deployment decision.
9. Using Benchmarks During Fine-Tuning

Tracking a relevant benchmark subset across fine-tuning checkpoints can help catch a specific, damaging failure mode, catastrophic forgetting of general capability while the model overfits narrowly to the fine-tuning task, a signal that per-task metrics alone would not necessarily reveal.
Worked Example

A team fine-tunes a model for customer support and, before deployment, runs it through MMLU and HellaSwag to check that general knowledge and reasoning capability have not degraded during the fine-tuning process.

They notice the fine-tuned model score on both benchmarks has dropped several points compared to the base model, a sign of catastrophic forgetting, prompting them to reduce the fine-tuning learning rate and add a small amount of general instruction data back into the training mix, after which a rerun of the same benchmarks shows scores recovering close to the base model original level.
Common Mistakes

items: Treating a high score on one benchmark as proof of strong general capability across all tasks
Comparing zero-shot and few-shot benchmark scores as if they were measuring the same thing
Ignoring the possibility of data contamination when a benchmark score looks unusually high
Relying only on standardized benchmarks and skipping task-specific evaluation against real production style data

blocks.text: Practice

Pick a fine-tuning task you are familiar with and identify one existing benchmark, from this topic or elsewhere, that would give a useful general capability sanity check alongside task-specific evaluation, then explain what specific risk, like catastrophic forgetting, that benchmark would help catch.
Key Takeaway

Benchmark evaluation runs a model against a fixed, standardized question set to produce a comparable score, useful for gauging general capability and catching regressions like catastrophic forgetting during fine-tuning, but it should be paired with task-specific evaluation and interpreted cautiously given the real risk of data contamination inflating reported scores.
